q: Child, low-grade fever, slow onset, seal-bark cough, stridor. What does this recap call it?

opts.why: Croup is viral in young kids: low-grade fever, slow onset, seal-bark cough, stridor.
Epiglottitis is high fever, rapid onset, tripod, and drooling, not a seal-bark.
Pertussis is coughing spells then a whoop on inspiration, not a seal-bark.
Flu has fever and cough with no unique bark or drool clue.

q: Child, high fever, rapid onset, stridor, tripod, drooling. What does this recap call it?

opts.why: Epiglottitis is bacterial, high fever, rapid onset, stridor, tripod, and drooling. The epiglottis can swell shut.
Croup is low-grade, slow, and seal-bark, not tripod and drooling.
Pertussis is the whoop after a coughing spell, not drooling and tripod.
Flu has no unique tripod-and-drool pattern.

q: Suspected epiglottitis. What does this recap say about the throat?

opts.why: Do not agitate. Avoid an oropharyngeal airway or suctioning the back of the throat. That can worsen swelling.
Do not suction the back of the throat in epiglottitis.

opts.t: Place an OPA in the throat
opts.why: Do not put an oropharyngeal airway in. It can worsen swelling.
Keep them very calm. Agitation can close the airway.

q: To hear stridor in this recap, do you need a stethoscope?

opts.why: Stridor is an upper-airway sound heard without a stethoscope. High-pitched on inspiration.
Lower sounds need a stethoscope. Stridor is audible without one.
Stridor is high-pitched on inspiration. Exhalation musical sound is wheeze.
Stridor is upper. Lower sounds are wheeze, rhonchi, and crackles.

q: Wheezing in this recap means what?

opts.why: Wheeze is musical, usually on exhalation, lower constriction (asthma, bronchiolitis, RSV, bronchitis). Needs a stethoscope.
Upper swelling is stridor, not wheeze.
That is rhonchi (low rattles), often pneumonia.
That is crackles, not wheeze.

q: Fever, colored sputum, and a localized abnormal lung sound. What does this recap call it?

opts.why: Fever, productive colored sputum, and a localized abnormal sound is pneumonia in this recap.
This recap’s localized colored-sputum pattern is pneumonia, not bronchitis.
Pulmonary edema is crackles from fluid in alveoli, not this colored-sputum infection picture.
Atelectasis is collapsed alveoli, not fever plus colored sputum.

q: Fever, night sweats, coughing up blood. What PPE does this recap want on you?

opts.why: TB triad is fever, night sweats, hemoptysis. N95/HEPA on you. Surgical mask on the patient.
Surgical mask goes on the patient. You need N95/HEPA.
Gloves and eye protection are not enough. This recap wants N95/HEPA on you.
This recap says N95/HEPA is a must. There is no US vaccine here.

q: Infant with RSV/bronchiolitis and a lot of mucus. What extra step does this recap want?

opts.why: Infants are nose-breathers. Suction the nose. It can make a big difference.
Do not skip suction. This recap wants you to suction the nose.
Oxygen as needed, but still suction the nose.
This recap’s RSV step is suction the nose, not the mouth first.

q: Infection plus which finding makes this recap call septic shock?

opts.why: Septic shock: evidence of infection plus hypotension. High-flow oxygen, warm, flat if tolerated, rapid transport.
The shock clue here is low pressure, not high.
Normal pressure is not septic shock in this recap. You need hypotension.
Fever is infection. Septic shock also needs low blood pressure.

q: Humidified oxygen is preferred for upper-airway infection. No humidifier. What then?

opts.why: Humidified is preferred. If you do not have it, still give dry oxygen. Hypoxia is worse than irritation.
Do not withhold oxygen waiting on a humidifier.
Give oxygen if they need it, even dry.
Start oxygen now. Do not wait for the hospital.

q: What does residual volume do in this recap?

opts.why: Residual volume is air left after a max exhale. It keeps alveoli open so the next breath does not have to pop them open.
Collapsed alveoli is atelectasis, the opposite of residual volume’s job.
Residual volume is about alveoli staying open, not filling the upper airway.
That is not residual volume. Residual volume keeps alveoli open.

q: Most dyspnea patients in this recap. How do you position them?

opts.why: Most short-of-breath patients sit up (Fowler/tripod). Supine is for shock with no respiratory compromise.
Supine is for shock if breathing is okay, not for most dyspnea.
This recap wants sitting up, not prone.
This recap does not put dyspnea patients head-down.
